newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Hutchison deal with Subic to be re-evaluated.
newsitem.headline: Hutchison deal with Subic to be re-evaluated.

text.p: Philippine President Fidel Ramos ordered the Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority (SBMA) on Tuesday to re-evaluate all bids for its container port privatisation project, presidential legal advisor Renato Cayetano said.
"The president expressed his concern that this matter be resolved as soon as possible," Renato Cayetano told reporters.

"The president ... directed the Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority to re-evaluate the financial bids submitted by ITCSI, Hutchison Ports Philippines Inc and Royal Ports Inc," a statement from the presidential palace said.

SBMA last month awarded a 25-year contract to develop and operate a container port at Subic, north of Manila, to a unit of Hutchison Whampoa Ltd after disqualifying the highest bidder, Philippine concern ICTSI Inc.
SBMA said it disqualified ICTSI, which also operates the Manila international container terminal, because it broke government rules against monopolies.
ICTSI protested over the ruling and Ramos intervened.
Cayetano said the president had also ordered SBMA to disregard arguments against monopolies.
ICTSI's bid was about $58 per twenty-foot equivalent unit (TEU), much higher than Hutchison's $20.50 per TEU and $15 per TEU by a third bidder, Royal Port Services Inc.
A Hutchison executive defended his company's bid, saying it offered more lucrative returns to the Philippines.
"If the tenders are taken in its totality, we are still the highest bidder," John Meredith, group managing director of Hutchison International Port Holdings Ltd, told a Manila news conference.
Meredith said Hutchison's tender had shown that it would handle many more containers than its rival bidders, generating more revenue for the Philippines.
"You can't simplistically look at the dollar figure. That's not how it works, you have to marry it with other things, like how many boxes you are going to carry," he said.
"We believe we offered the best deal. We promised to invest $60 million up front and also committed to put in another $120 million over the next eight years," he said.
Meredith said he was concerned the revaluation of the bids ordered by the government would not look at the total picture but just at the amount quoted.
